title: object, CTS, and dynamic
hook: `object` is the CTS root — every value can be treated as one (boxing if needed). `dynamic` is a compiler conspiracy to emit run-time binding. It is not TypeScript `any`, and it is not `unknown`.

sections.heading: Unified hierarchy versus late binding
sections.prose: The Common Type System says all types derive from `System.Object`. Value types inherit `System.ValueType` then `object`. That is why a `List<object>` can hold an `int` (boxed) and a `string`. Useful for heterogeneous logging; costly if you meant a generic. `dynamic` turns member access into a run-time binder (`Microsoft.CSharp.RuntimeBinder`). Typos compile; they throw at run time. JSON libraries sometimes expose `dynamic` — prefer `JsonElement` or a DTO for auth tokens. TypeScript `any` disables checking and erases; `unknown` forces you to narrow. C# `object` still requires casts/`is`; `dynamic` skips compile-time member checking. There is no C# `unknown`. When a RabbitMQ payload is `object`, you immediately `is` it into a typed message.

snippets.label: object needs a test; dynamic fails late
snippets.explanation: Wrong: `dynamic` as a substitute for generics. Wrong: calling `dynamic` the same as TS `any` without mentioning the DLR binder and extra dependency.

interviewTakeaways: CTS: one object hierarchy; boxing is how values enter it.
`object` is statically typed as object; you must convert to use members.
`dynamic` is compile-time `object`-ish with run-time binding — closer to `any` than to `unknown`, but it is still a .NET feature with a binder.
commonPitfalls: Using `dynamic` for JSON because it “feels like JS.”
Storing value types in `object` collections and creating boxing traffic.
Saying C# has `any` — it does not; say `object` or `dynamic` and know the difference.

jsTsCorrelations.note: `any` skips checks and erases. `unknown` must be narrowed. C# `object` is a real type you cast; `dynamic` skips member checks but still runs on the CLR binder.
